Niels Lyhne had a habit of reflection that hobbled him. It sprang from an instinctive retreat from decisive acts, and behind that instinct lay an unacknowledged feeling that he had no personality. He fought this reflective habit continually, sometimes lashing himself with ugly names for it, sometimes dressing it up as a virtue rooted in his deepest being and inseparable from all his powers and prospects. Yet whatever he called it, from whatever side he considered it, he hated it as a hidden disability. He might conceal it from everyone else, but could never conceal it from himself; whenever he was alone, it was there to shame him. How he envied the boldness that flings itself confidently into speech, without considering that speech entails actions and actions entail consequences, until the consequences come running after it. Those who had that boldness looked to him like centaurs, horse and man poured into one mould. For them the urge and the leap were a single thing; he, meanwhile, remained horse and rider separately, with the impulse here and the leap somewhere quite different.

Whenever he imagined telling Mrs. Boye that he loved her—and everything had to be imagined beforehand—he saw himself distinctly in the scene: his posture, each movement, his entire body viewed from behind, in profile, and face-on. He watched himself hesitate in that fever of indecision which scattered his wits and left him helpless. There he would stand, waiting for her reply as though it must be a stroke that brought him to his knees, when it might instead be a shuttlecock, something he could send back a hundred different ways and receive again in a hundred others.

He considered telling her aloud; he considered putting it in a letter; but he could never just let the words come out. He expressed it only through disguised avowals and a partly acted lyrical ardour, pretending to be swept into burning speeches and extravagant hopes. Still, a peculiar intimacy began to form between them, made from a young man's reverent love, a dreamer's passionate yearning, and a woman's delight in being the unattainable goal of romantic desire. Their attachment assumed the shape of a myth; neither could have said how it arose, this quiet, colourless myth born in a drawing-room. The central figure was a beautiful woman who, when very young, had loved a great man of the intellect. He had left her and died abroad, abandoned and forgotten. Through long years the beautiful woman mourned him, though nobody knew her pain; only solitude was holy enough to witness her sorrow. At last a young man appeared, who revered the dead thinker as his master, who breathed his spirit and burned with enthusiasm for his work. This young man loved the grieving woman. She felt her happy days, long buried, rise out of their grave into life. A strange, delicious confusion possessed her. The present and the past dissolved together in the silver haze of a dim, dreamlike day, where she loved the young man partly for himself and partly as another man's likeness, and surrendered half her soul to him. He, however, must move cautiously, or the bubble of the dream would break. He must keep a firm barrier against every burning, earthly desire, or he would drive away that gentle twilight and awaken her again to grief.

Under the protection of this myth, their intimacy slowly settled into an established shape. Alone together they used their first names, becoming Niels and Tema, and the niece's appearances were kept as brief as possible. Niels did sometimes attempt to cross the agreed boundaries, certainly; but Mrs. Boye had so much more power that she could put down these little rebellions with effortless gentleness. He had to yield, and content himself for another while with an imaginary passion acted out in real tableaux. Their attachment never dwindled into a dull platonic affair, nor subsided into the sleepy sameness of custom. Sleep or rest had very little to do with it. Niels Lyhne never exhausted his hope. Whenever it blazed into a demand, she softly smothered it, but that only sent it burning more fiercely underground. And with what endless flirtations Mrs. Boye stoked the fire, with her disarming frankness and her fearless freedom in speaking of the most intimate matters! Nor did she control every move in this game. At times, in her idle blood, she dreamed of rewarding his imperfectly subdued devotion with all the ecstasy love could give, so that she might enjoy his astonished bliss. Such a dream did not readily fade. When Niels next appeared, she would receive him with the uneasiness of someone aware of sin, the timid air of a guilty woman, a delicious embarrassment that set a strange vibration of passion in the air.

Something else, too, kept a tension alive between them. There was enough manly strength in Niels Lyhne's love to make him chivalrously refuse to seize in fantasy what actual life withheld. Even in that private realm where everything obeyed his wishes, he treated Mrs. Boye with the respect he would have shown if she were truly there.

Their attachment thus had solid supports on either side, with no prospect of its immediate collapse. Indeed, it might have been devised for someone of Niels Lyhne's temperament, so reflective and yet so thirsty for life. A game it might be, but its pieces were real, and it supplied all the hidden current of passion that he required.

Niels Lyhne had resolved to become a poet, and many of the outward conditions of his life encouraged his mind that way and roused the abilities the work demanded. As yet, though, his dreams were almost his only subject, and nothing is more repetitive or more monotonous than imagination. That country of dreams looks limitless and endlessly various; in reality it contains only a handful of short, well-trodden tracks, along which everyone travels without ever stepping aside. Individuals differ from one another, but their dreams do not. In dreams they invariably secure the three or four things they want, more swiftly or slowly, more fully or less fully, but in the end they secure them. Nobody seriously pictures himself coming away empty-handed. Consequently, nobody discovers who he is in his dreams, or learns from them the particular character of his own being. Dreams do not tell us what satisfaction we find in the treasure once won, how we surrender it when it is lost, what enjoyment we draw from possessing it, or where we go when it is snatched away.

Until now, Niels Lyhne's poems had merely voiced an aesthetic personality that held, in a general sort of way, that spring was abundant, the sea immense, love sensual, and death sad. The poems contained nothing of himself; he was only the person who arranged the lines. This now began to change. He was courting a woman, and he wanted her to love him: Niels Lyhne from Lönborggaard, aged twenty-three, with a slight stoop, fine hands, little ears, and a somewhat shy disposition. It was this man he wanted loved, rather than the splendid Nicolaus of his fantasies, a slightly older man with a commanding posture and an assured manner. So he began to feel a living interest in this Niels, whose company he had previously endured as one puts up with a friend who is not quite fit to introduce. He had spent so much time adorning himself with virtues he did not own that he had never paused to notice those he did. Now he started assembling his own character out of fragments of childhood recollection and impression, and the most intensely remembered moments of his life. With delighted surprise he watched the pieces join and fuse, little by little, into a personality far more intimately known than the one he had pursued in fancy. This person was infinitely more real, stronger, and more richly gifted. Here was no lifeless remnant of an ideal, but a living being through which innumerable changing possibilities moved, giving it a unity of a thousand forms. Good God, he _did_ have gifts that were useful exactly as they were! He _was_ Aladdin: everything he had besieged the heavens to obtain had already dropped straight into his turban.

A joyful season followed for Niels: that magnificent season when the strong current of growth bears us triumphantly over the stagnant places in our character. Strength swells inside us until we feel ready to set our shoulders against mountains, if necessary, and boldly continue building our Tower of Babel. We mean it to thrust through heaven; it ends as a low, squat building, to which we spend the rest of our lives making additions, a hesitant little spire today, an eccentric projecting window tomorrow.

All was different now. His character, his gifts, and his work meshed like the teeth of interlocking wheels. Pausing to admire his art never occurred to him. As soon as he finished something he threw it aside, having already grown beyond it in the course of making it. It was only another stair towards a goal that kept withdrawing, one among many stairs on a road already behind him, forgotten even as the sound of his steps still rang along it.

New desires and thoughts carried him towards greater strength and a wider view, and in the process he became steadily more alone. His former companions dropped away one after another and disappeared from sight. They ceased to interest him as the distinction grew fainter between these professed rebels and the majority they assailed. Everything seemed to run together into a vast, hostile bulk of tediousness. What, after all, did they produce when they sounded the charge? Gloomy poems announcing that dogs frequently showed more loyalty than people, and convicts more honesty than men at liberty; sonorous odes explaining that green forests and brown heath were better than dusty towns; tales contrasting peasants' goodness with wealthy men's wickedness, vigorous nature with bloodless civilization, old people's cramped outlook with youth's divine entitlement. How little they asked for once they put pen to paper! At least in conversation, safely enclosed by four walls, they dared rather more.
When his own moment arrived, he would give them something to hear: a trumpet sounding the advance!

His earlier friendships also began to suffer, above all his friendship with Frithjof. Frithjof had a decisive temperament, a head well suited to systems, and shoulders broad enough to carry dogmas. He had, in fact, read rather too much Heiberg and swallowed the whole as revealed truth. It never occurred to him that system-builders were ingenious people who constructed their systems out of their books, instead of constructing books out of systems. Young people who pledge allegiance to a system notoriously become formidable dogmatists, thanks to youth's often admirable fondness for things complete and bounded. Besides, once the entire truth belongs to you, keeping it to yourself would be inexcusable. Surely you cannot leave your less fortunate neighbours to wander down their mistaken paths. You must guide and educate them, cut back their straying shoots with affectionate firmness, press them against the wall with considerate force, and show them the prescribed lines of growth. Then one day, shaped into properly trained and artistically arranged espaliers, they will thank you for your pains, even if their gratitude comes rather late.

Niels liked to announce that nothing pleased him more than criticism; in reality he liked admiration better. Criticism from Frithjof was especially intolerable. He had always considered Frithjof his dependent, and Frithjof had always been happy enough to put on the uniform of Niels's principles and beliefs. Yet now he proposed to act as an equal, parading about in a cloak he had chosen himself! Naturally he had to be put in his place. Niels began with an air of genial superiority, trying to make Frithjof see himself as ridiculous. When this failed, he resorted to outrageous paradoxes which he contemptuously refused to argue about. He simply flung them down in their grotesque ugliness and withdrew into a silence designed to irritate.
That was how the distance between them widened.

Things went better between him and Erik. Even as boys, their friendship had maintained a little distance, a sort of modesty of the spirit. This had protected it from the excessive familiarity that so readily endangers friendship. They had shared enthusiasms in their souls' banqueting hall and talked confidentially in the drawing-room, but neither had presumed to wander into the other's bedrooms, bathrooms, or the other private chambers of that inward house.

That was still true. If anything, their reserve had increased, particularly on Niels's side; yet it did not diminish their friendship. Its foundation remained what it had always been: Niels Lyhne's admiration for Erik's lively courage and daring, his apparent ease with life, his promptness in reaching out and taking hold. Nevertheless, Niels could not disguise from himself how unequal the friendship was. Erik certainly did not lack genuine love for him or confidence in him; quite the reverse. Nobody esteemed Niels more highly. Erik thought him so immeasurably above himself in intellectual matters that criticism never entered his head. But this unquestioning reverence made him set Niels, his activities, and his interests far outside the horizon visible to himself. He felt certain Niels would travel a long way on his chosen road; he felt just as certain that his own feet had no business there, and never even tried to follow.

This seemed rather unfair to Niels. Erik's ideals were not his own, and the romanticism, or romantic sentimentality, that Erik sought to embody in his art was foreign to his convictions. Yet Niels could summon a more generous sympathy, enabling him to keep faithful track of his friend's progress, to celebrate every advance with him, and to sustain his hope when he made no headway.

Such was the inequality in their friendship. It was hardly surprising that Niels became aware of what was missing just when his own mind was wrestling with unfamiliar ideas and he needed someone sympathetic into whose ears he could pour his thoughts. The discovery embittered him. He began to inspect more critically the friend he had always treated with such indulgence. A bleak loneliness settled over him as he saw everything brought from home and the old days slipping away, leaving him to make his way abandoned and unremembered. The door into his past was bolted; he stood on the threshold alone, with nothing in his hands. Whatever he wanted, whatever he required, he would have to obtain by his own efforts: other friends, another refuge, fresh affections, and fresh memories.
For over a year Mrs. Boye had been the sole person who truly shared Niels's life. Then his mother wrote that his father was gravely ill, and her letter summoned him home to Lönborggaard.
His father had died before he reached home.

Niels felt almost criminal when he remembered how little he had missed his home during the past several years. His mind had visited it often, certainly, but always as a traveller, carrying other countries' dust on his clothing and other places' recollections in his heart. He had never ached for it with fierce homesickness, as the lovely refuge of his existence; he had never yearned to kiss its ground or lie beneath its roof. He now regretted that disloyalty to his home. Under the weight of grief, his regret deepened into a dim sense of complicity, as if his faithlessness had somehow opened the door to death. How had he ever been happy living away from a place that drew him now with such mysterious force? Every part of him clung to it in a boundless, desolate yearning. He was restless because he could not unite himself with it as completely as he wished; miserable because the innumerable memories calling to him from every bush and corner, from noises and countless smells, from shifting light and even from silence, all spoke from so far away. He could not seize them in the full intensity he longed for. They only murmured within him, like the rustle of leaves descending to earth, or the little splash of water passing onward, always onward....

Fortunate in grief is anyone who, losing a beloved person, can spend every tear on vacancy, desolation, and solitude alone. Far more painful and bitter are the tears offered in payment for the past, when you withheld love from someone now gone, someone to whom you can never repair the wrong. Everything returns then. The cruel words return, the answers delicately tainted with poison, the merciless condemnation, the senseless rage; and so do the unspoken unkindnesses, the swift judgments that only crossed your mind, the unnoticed shrug, the concealed smile of impatience and contempt. They fly back like spiteful arrows and drive their barbs deep into your breast. Their barbs are blunt: their sharp points have broken off in the heart that no longer lives. You can put nothing right now, nothing at all. Love fills your heart at last, when at last it is too late. Take that overflowing heart to the cold grave! Does it close the distance? Set flowers there, weave wreaths: will either bring relief?

Wreaths were being woven at Lönborggaard. There, too, people remembered with anguish the moments when rougher voices had drowned out love. There, too, the grave's tightly closed mouth, with its severe lines, seemed to speak to them of remorse.

The time was shadowed and sorrowful, yet one brightness lay within it: mother and son drew nearer than they had been in many long years. For all their deep affection, they had always kept a kind of watch on each other. A restraint had entered their dealings from the day Niels became too big for his mother's lap. Her nervous excitability had made him draw back, while his hesitations and shyness had seemed to her something foreign. Now life itself, which raises the pitch and lowers it and brings things into harmony, had made their hearts ready. Soon it would let them belong entirely to one another.

Less than two months after the burial, Mrs. Lyhne became desperately ill, and for many days her survival remained doubtful. The worry of those weeks pushed their previous sorrow aside. By the time she began to mend, both she and Niels felt as though years had intervened between themselves and that newly dug grave. To Mrs. Lyhne especially, the interval seemed immense. During her illness she had believed she would die, and death had terrified her. Now recovery had started and the doctor pronounced her out of danger; even so, she could not shake off the dark thoughts that possessed her.

Her recovery was dispiriting. Strength seemed to trickle back unwillingly, a drop at a time. Instead of the soft, restorative sleepiness of healing, she felt an agitated weariness, a crushing awareness of weakness, and a continual, helpless craving to be strong again.

Eventually this altered. She improved more quickly and regained her strength. But the belief that she must soon leave life remained. It cast a shadow across her, holding her imprisoned in a melancholy full of longing and unease.

One evening she sat by herself in the summer sitting-room, looking through the doors, which stood wide open. The garden trees screened the sunset's crimson and gold. At one point, though, a gap between the trunks exposed a patch of flaming sky. From it long shafts of rich golden sunlight spread outward, bringing out green colours and brown-bronze gleams in the dark masses of leaves.

Far over the tossing treetops, clouds moved like dark shapes across the smoky red heavens. In their haste they shed small wisps behind them, slender scraps of cloud that the sun saturated with the glow of wine.

Mrs. Lyhne listened to the wind moving in the branches. Her head stirred almost imperceptibly to the irregular rise and fall of each gust, as it rushed towards her, swept noisily through, and faded. Her gaze, however, was distant, farther away even than the clouds before her eyes. Dressed in her widow's black, she sat pale, with a touching look of uneasiness around her barely pink lips. Her fingers kept playing with the small, thick volume in her lap: Rousseau's _Héloïse_. More books lay stacked about her, Schiller, Staffeldt, Evald, and Novalis, together with broad portfolios of engravings showing ancient churches, ruined buildings, and lakes among mountains.

Doors began to open and close. Footsteps followed, apparently searching the rooms farther inside for someone; a moment later Niels entered. He had taken a long walk beside the fjord. The outdoor air had reddened his cheeks, and his hair still showed the wind's disorder.
Outdoors, blue-grey shades had taken possession of the heavens. A handful of large raindrops struck the window glass.

Niels described the great waves rolling ashore and the seaweed they had thrown onto the beach, then spoke of the people he had encountered and the things he had noticed. While telling her, he collected the books, shut the garden doors, and secured the windows. Finally he settled onto the little stool beside his mother's feet, held her hand, and rested his face against her knee.
Outside it was almost pitch-dark now. Rain rattled down like hailstones, streaming across the window frames and glass.

After a long quiet pause Niels said, “Can you remember how we used to sit this way at twilight, setting off to find adventures? Father would be in his office discussing things with Jens Overseer, and we could hear Duysen clattering the tea things in the dining-room. When they brought the lamp, both of us would come back from our extraordinary adventures into the safe warmth of the room. But I remember perfectly how I always believed the tale continued after we stopped, carrying on somewhere underneath the hills along the Ringkjöbing road.”
He could not see the longing in his mother's smile, but he felt the soft movement of her hand across his hair.
A little later she asked, “Can you remember all those promises you made, that once you were grown you would sail away in a great ship and come home with every treasure in the world for me?”

“How could I forget! There were to be hyacinths, because you were so fond of them, and a palm to replace the one that died, and gold and marble pillars. Your stories were always full of pillars, so many of them. Do you remember those?”

“I've waited for that ship. No, darling, don't move; you haven't understood. I wasn't waiting for gifts for myself: I meant the ship that would carry your destiny.... I wanted you to have a splendid, full life, to walk along radiant roads.... Renown, everything. No, I don't mean that, only that you should join the people who struggle for the highest things. I can't explain it, but ordinary happiness and ordinary ambitions make me so weary. Can you understand?”

“You wanted a Sunday child for your son, dear mother: someone who doesn't have to share the common harness, someone with a heaven of his own for his salvation and a private hell for his damnation as well. We were going to carry flowers in our ship, weren't we? Wonderful flowers to scatter across a dreary world. Only the ship never arrived, and a sorry pair of birds they were, Niels and his mother, weren't they?”
“Darling, have I wounded you? They were only dreams, after all; don't let them trouble you!”

For a long while Niels said nothing, embarrassed by the words he wanted to speak. At last he began: “Mother, we aren't as badly off as you believe. The ship will reach us one day. If only you could trust that, and put your trust in me.... Mother, I am a poet, truly, in every part of my soul. Don't suppose these are a child's fantasies, or fantasies nourished on conceit. If you could know the thankful pride I feel in whatever is finest in me, the humble happiness with which I say this, so free of self, so distant from boasting, you would believe exactly what I want you to believe. My dearest, dearest mother! I _will_ join those who struggle for the highest things, and I give you my word that I won't betray them, that I will remain true to myself and to my gift. I will accept nothing less than the best. There can be no compromise, mother! If I test my work's weight and find the metal isn't pure, or strike it and hear a crack, a fault, back it goes into the crucible! Each thing I make must be the finest I can make! Do you understand why I must pledge myself? Gratitude for what I possess compels me to make these promises, and you must be the one to hear them. If I break them, I will have wronged you. It is you who made my soul a room with a soaring vault. Your wishes and your dreams set its growth in motion; your responsiveness and your unfulfilled hunger for beauty dedicated me to the work of my life.”

Mrs. Lyhne's tears fell without a sound. She could feel delight draining the colour from her face. She gently set both hands upon her son's head; he softly brought them down to his mouth and kissed them.

“Niels, you've given me such happiness! My whole life hasn't simply been a long, fruitless sigh, then, if I've helped you forward as I so passionately wished and imagined—heaven knows how often I imagined it! How often! And still, Niels, there's so much sorrow woven through my happiness! To have the wish dearest to me granted, the one I've cherished for all these years.... Things like that only happen when one's life is nearly over.”
“Don't say such things, you mustn't! Everything is turning out well, and you're gaining strength day by day, dear mother, aren't you?”

“Dying is so difficult,” she murmured. “Can you guess what filled my mind through those long nights without sleep, when death felt so frightfully close? What seemed most bitter was knowing how much that was magnificent and beautiful lay out in the world, and that I would have to leave it all unseen. I thought of the countless souls those things had raised up and flooded with joy and life, when for me they might never have existed. I felt my soul would take flight like a pauper on frail wings, carrying no golden recollections, no reflected brightness from the splendours of its native country, because it had spent its time beside the hearth hearing tales of the marvellous world. Niels, nobody can conceive the torment of being shut inside a dreary, darkened sickroom, trying with a fevered imagination to summon the loveliness of countries one has never visited: the white summits of the Alps above lakes of deepest blue, shining rivers flowing between vineyards, long mountain ranges where ruins show among the trees, and then immense rooms peopled with gods of marble. You never quite manage it; you abandon it and begin again, because leaving without the smallest share in it seems so cruelly hard.... Oh God, Niels, to crave it with your entire being and feel yourself being carried, slowly, towards the entrance of another world; to pause on that threshold looking back, looking so long, while something drives you through a doorway beyond which none of your desires have ever travelled.... When your turn comes to enjoy that splendour, darling, take me with you in your thoughts, into all that I will never, never be allowed to see!”
Her tears came.

Niels did what he could to soothe her. He devised ambitious journeys they would make together once her health was fully restored. He would visit a doctor in the city, he said, and surely the doctor would agree that travel was the very best course. Hadn't so-and-so gone away and come back entirely cured, simply because of the change? A change could often accomplish miracles. He laid out their itinerary down to its smallest particulars: the warm clothes he would bundle her in, the brief stages they would travel at first, the entertaining diary they would write. They would observe every tiny detail. How amusing it would be to dine on the oddest dishes in the most beautiful settings, and what dreadful crimes against grammar they would commit to begin with.

He talked like this through the whole evening and the succeeding days, without tiring of it. She joined him in the project as she might join in an agreeable daydream, though she clearly believed it could never actually happen.

Niels nevertheless followed the doctor's counsel and continued arranging everything their journey would require. She allowed him his way, even letting him choose their departure date, certain that _the thing_ would occur which must wreck all his preparations. But at last the date was only a few days away. Her youngest brother, who would run the farm while they were gone, had actually arrived. Her certainty began to waver, and now she was the one impatient to leave. Somewhere in her mind the fear still hid that, at the final instant, the obstacle would spring up and block their road.
And so they departed.

On their first day she remained fretful and anxious, with some residue of the old dread. Only after the day ended safely could she begin to believe that she truly was travelling towards the wonders she had wanted so desperately. A fever of happiness seized her then. Exuberant expectation coloured everything she said or thought, and her mind returned ceaselessly to the gifts the days ahead would bring, each in its turn.

Everything did indeed arrive, everything she had wished for. Yet it neither transported her nor stirred her with the force and warmth she had anticipated. She had pictured the sights differently, and herself differently too. In poetry and in dreams it had all lain, so to speak, across the sea. A veil of distance had mysteriously covered the restless confusion of particulars, leaving the great outlines clear and strong, while the hush of that distance supplied its enchantment. Beauty had been easy to receive then. Now she stood among these things, with every small detail asserting itself and clamouring in reality's many voices. Beauty broke apart like light passing through a prism, and she could not reunite its scattered beams; she could not set the picture back across the sea. In discouragement she had to acknowledge how poor she felt, hemmed in by riches she was unable to possess.

She wanted to press onward, always farther, hoping for somewhere she could recognize as a fragment of her imagined world. Yet every step towards that world appeared to put out the magical radiance around it. Before her disappointed gaze it spread in the ordinary illumination of the sun and moon that shone for everyone. Her search brought nothing. The year was getting late, and they hurried to Clarens, where the doctor recommended passing the winter. One last weak glimmer of hope also drew her there, that weary soul still wrapped in dreams. Was this not Rousseau's Clarens, Julie's Paradise!

They stayed there. Winter softened his manner and withheld his icy breath from her, but without effect; he had no remedy for the fever in her veins. When Spring made his victorious progress through the valley, bringing the miracle of germinating seeds and the good news of unfolding leaves, he too was forced to go past her, leaving her to fade amid all that lavish rebirth. Light, air, earth, and water sent strength pouring towards her, but it would not turn to strength inside her. It could neither intoxicate her blood with health nor make it lift its joyful voice in the mighty hymn to Spring's all-powerful rule. She could only fade. That final dream, which in her shadowed home had risen like the red promise of dawn, the dream of the far world's splendours, had brought no daylight after it. As she approached, its colours grew fainter. She knew they looked faint because the colours she had wanted were absent from life, because the beauty she craved could never ripen on earth. Yet her desire did not die. Quietly and fiercely it burned within her, fiercer for its unsatisfied thirst, a heat that consumed her.

Spring held his festival around her, heavy with the promise of beauty. The white bells of snowdrops rang it open; crocuses raised their delicately veined cups in joyful greeting. Hundreds of little streams flung themselves down the mountains into the valley, hurrying to announce Spring's arrival. Too late, all of them: as they slipped between green banks, yellow primroses and blue violets nodded to them, saying, We know it, we know it; we knew before you did! Willows opened yellow flags. Curling ferns and velvet moss draped the bare vineyard walls with green festoons, while beneath them dry nettles concealed the stones behind long edgings of brown, green, and a trace of purple. Grass laid its green cloak over the land, and lovely flowers beyond counting settled on it: hyacinths carrying star-shaped flowers and pearl-shaped flowers, crowds of daisies, gentians, anemones, dandelions, and a hundred more. Above the blossoms at ground level, a thousand brilliant islands of flowers seemed to float in the air, held aloft by the grey trunks of ancient cherry trees. Light broke in foam along their white coasts, where red and blue butterflies alighted, bearing news from the continent of flowers below.

Each new day pushed more flowers from the soil, weaving coloured designs in the gardens beside the water and spilling blossoms over the trees there: paullinias resembling enormous violets, magnolias like gigantic tulips stained purple. Flowers marched beside the pathways in ranks of white and blue, and crowded the fields in yellow hosts. But the thickest abundance filled the small protected valleys higher in the hills. There larches displayed cones like sparkling rubies against their pale needles, and narcissi opened in dazzling multitudes, sending the heavy, sleep-inducing perfume of their white revels far through the air.

Surrounded by such loveliness, she still sat with the same old hunger for beauty unanswered within her. Only occasionally could nature enchant her senses: when the sun dropped behind Savoy's soft slopes, and the mountains across the water looked like dark brown glass that admitted no light, as if their sheer faces had absorbed it all. Then evening's luminous yellow haze would hide the far-off Jura Mountains. The lake became a copper looking-glass, sending tongues of golden fire into the sunset's red radiance, until water and sky seemed to dissolve into a single shining boundlessness. At such moments, very rarely, it seemed her longing had fallen quiet and her soul had reached the country it had been seeking.

As the spring wore on, she grew steadily weaker. Before long she could no longer rise from bed. But death had ceased to frighten her: she looked forward to it impatiently. She hoped that on the other side of the grave she would meet all that magnificence face to face, that her soul would merge with the complete beauty that had called her through earthly hope and longing. The mounting pain of long, unfulfilled years had purified and transformed that longing, making it ready at last to achieve its end. She dreamed many soft, wistful dreams of remembering what the earth had offered her, returning to it in thought from immortality's country, where every earthly beauty would forever lie across the sea.

And so her life ended. Niels laid her to rest in the welcoming churchyard of Clarens, where the brown soil of the vineyards lies over people born in many countries, and where broken pillars and draped urns speak the same grief in so many different tongues.

White, they shine beneath the dark cypresses and amid the viburnum's winter flowers. Early roses scatter petals on many of them, and violets often colour the earth at their feet blue. Yet across every stone and mound the soft periwinkle trails its glossy leaves, Rousseau's beloved flower, blue with a sky-blue deeper than any sky has ever worn.
